title: Worksheet — The Rise of Nationalism in Europe (Class 10 CBSE History)
instructions: Attempt all 11 questions. Show your reasoning where required. Total time: 50 minutes.

questions.question: Frédéric Sorrieu's 1848 prints visualised a world made up of:
Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 did NOT:
Greece won independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1832.
Italy's volunteer leader who marched into the south in 1860 was ____.
The female allegory of GERMANY wears a crown of:
Why did initial enthusiasm for the French armies later give way to hostility?
options: the French armies brought no reforms
because of conscription, censorship, increased taxation and loss of political freedoms
because they spoke a different language
questions.answer: because of conscription, censorship, increased taxation and loss of political freedoms

questions.question: What measures did the French revolutionaries take to create a sense of collective identity among the French?
questions.answer: They emphasised la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen). They introduced the tricolour flag, replaced the Estates General with an elected National Assembly, set up uniform laws and a centralised administration, abolished internal customs duties, adopted uniform weights and measures, and made Parisian French the common national language.

questions.question: What role did the educated middle class and the Romantic movement play in spreading 19th-century nationalism?
questions.answer: The new educated middle class — entrepreneurs, professionals, students — championed liberty, equality before the law and constitutional government, and led nationalist movements. ROMANTICISM emphasised emotion and folk culture; thinkers like Herder argued that the true spirit of a nation lived in its language, songs and folk traditions. Together the middle class gave nationalism its political programme and the Romantics its emotional and cultural power.

questions.question: Briefly describe how Italy was unified.
questions.answer: Italy was politically fragmented into seven states. Mazzini's 'Young Italy' movement failed. Then the Sardinian king Victor Emmanuel II and his minister Cavour, with French alliance, defeated Austria in 1859. Garibaldi led armed volunteers into South Italy in 1860 and won over the local peasants, driving out the Spanish Bourbons. In 1861, Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of UNITED ITALY.

questions.question: Discuss the major liberal-nationalist uprisings of 1830 and 1848 in Europe. To what extent were they successful?
questions.answer: 1830s — economic hardship, population growth, urban migration and feudal dues combined with the demand for liberal-nationalist constitutions. The JULY REVOLUTION in France (1830) overthrew the Bourbons and installed Louis Philippe; Belgium broke away from the Netherlands; Greece won independence (Treaty of Constantinople, 1832). 1848 — fresh food shortages and unemployment triggered uprisings in Paris, Vienna, Berlin and Italian states. Workers and peasants demanded relief; the educated middle classes pressed for nationalist constitutions. In Frankfurt, an all-German parliament drafted a constitution; it was rejected by Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia and the assembly was dispersed. ASSESSMENT — most 1848 revolutions were politically defeated, but they made the demand for constitutional, liberal nation-states impossible to ignore. The actual unification of Italy and Germany came two decades later — through conservative state-building rather than liberal revolution.

questions.question: Trace how nationalism in Europe shifted from a liberal-democratic ideal in the early 19th century to a narrow, imperialist creed by the end of the century. Use specific examples.
questions.answer: EARLY 19TH CENTURY — nationalism was linked with LIBERTY and DEMOCRACY: constitutional government, equality before the law, civil rights, the abolition of feudal privileges. The 1830 and 1848 revolutions, the Greek war of independence and Mazzini's Young Italy expressed this liberal ideal. SECOND HALF — nationalism was harnessed by CONSERVATIVES for STATE-BUILDING: Bismarck's wars (1864/1866/1870-71) and Cavour's diplomacy unified Germany and Italy without democratic revolution. New states emphasised modern administration, modern armies and economic uniformity, but were not especially democratic. LATE 19TH CENTURY — nationalism became a NARROW CREED: groups grew intolerant of one another and ever ready to go to war. European powers manipulated subject peoples' nationalisms in the Balkans for IMPERIALIST aims; Balkan states were jealous of each other; great-power rivalry over trade, colonies and arms grew sharper. These rivalries detonated in the FIRST WORLD WAR (1914). The same word — NATIONALISM — moved from a call for FREEDOM in 1789–1848 to a call for EMPIRE AND WAR by 1900.
